justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with a modest upward drift over longer horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 21.45 is anchored closely to what would be a recent observed price or level, assuming mean-reverting behavior dominates over very short windows and that no major catalyst is imminent. At the one-week horizon, the slight uptick to 21.5 reflects a marginal positive drift assumption, consistent with modest bullish momentum or a slight upward trend in the underlying series. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 21.65 incorporates a continuation of that drift, though the signal becomes increasingly diluted by noise and uncertainty the further out we project.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds with time. At one day, the 90% interval of 21.0 to 21.9 is quite tight, as short-term price dynamics tend to be relatively predictable absent shock events, and realized volatility over a single session is limited. By one week, the interval widens to 20.6–22.4, capturing the possibility of a meaningful swing driven by macroeconomic data releases, sentiment shifts, or technical breakouts. At one month, the interval of 19.8–23.5 is substantially wider, acknowledging that over four weeks a variety of fundamental and technical factors can shift the underlying level materially in either direction. The asymmetry between downside and upside in the monthly interval is roughly balanced, suggesting no strong skew in my prior.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in risk sentiment — triggered by an unexpected policy shift, geopolitical escalation, or a disappointing macroeconomic print — could breach the lower bound of even the monthly interval. Liquidity events or forced selling in correlated assets could amplify moves beyond what historical volatility would suggest. On the upside, a positive surprise in earnings, economic data, or a dovish central bank pivot could drive a sharp rally that exceeds the upper bound. Tail risks by definition are underweighted in any interval constructed from recent realized volatility, so black swan events remain a genuine source of interval violation risk across all three horizons.
